title: Most 'alpha' in fixed income is credit spread beta
dek: NISA's CEO says most of what the industry calls fixed-income alpha shrinks dramatically when measured against credit benchmarks; it's systematic credit overweighting—beta, not genuine skill.
why: This episode is information-dense, with rigorous unpacking of fixed-income alpha fundamentals, private credit leverage structures, and pension LDI mechanics. Worth hearing in full; the opening personal history can be skipped.
who: Institutional investors managing pensions or fixed-income portfolios; allocation investors focused on private credit structural risks; and quants trying to understand whether ‘alpha’ is really disguised beta.
skip: The opening personal education and career narrative (approximately 0:00–20:00) can be skipped without losing the investment arguments that follow.

points.h: Most industry 'alpha' is actually credit beta
points.body: David Eichhorn points out that many fixed-income managers outperform the Bloomberg Aggregate Index because that index is half Treasuries—an asset class "hard to enhance"—so managers overweight credit bonds, ABS, and high-yield debt to beat it. When those excess returns are measured against credit-only indices or S&P benchmarks, they shrink dramatically, revealing that managers are simply long credit systematically and shouldn't collect active management fees. NISA's approach removes that 50% Treasury "seductive problem" from the benchmark, making it harder, so the outperformance they deliver is genuine skill-based excess return.

points.h: Fixed income is easier to fake outperformance than equities
points.body: Beating the stock market long-term is rare; genuine practitioners appear once a generation. Fixed income is different. Managers can quietly overweight credit spreads—sell Treasuries, buy corporates—and generate consistent outperformance until a credit spread blowout (an ‘air pocket’ moment) exposes them. The 2008 financial crisis revealed this strategy's true face, but the Fed's rapid COVID rescue re-buried the problem.

points.h: Real alpha can be found trading bonds from the same issuer
points.body: A stock has one ticker in the S&P; the same issuer (say, AT&T) may have fifty to sixty different CUSIPs in bond indices, priced differently due to over-the-counter trading. NISA trades within the same issuer's bond complex—swapping underpriced cheap bonds for overpriced expensive ones—earning pure spread on the same credit risk. This is among their highest information-ratio alpha sources.

points.h: AI megacaps, not government, are pushing up Treasury yields
points.body: The conventional story is government debt crowding out private investors. This time, AI megacaps' issuance rivals nation-building capital needs; they're crowding out others and pushing rates up continuously. These issuers' credit spreads have widened, but most are highly profitable with no near-term default risk. Spread widening is purely from their relentless new issuance and persistent market pressure.

points.h: Market still trusts the Fed on inflation; real rates are rising
points.body: Despite tariff shocks and war-driven oil prices, the break-even inflation rate between TIPS and nominal Treasuries remains just above 2% on the long end, signaling markets still trust the Fed's inflation control. With nominal yields rising but inflation expectations flat, real rates are climbing—30-year real Treasury yields near 3.5%, which he views as unreasonably high for the current economy.

points.h: Private credit is fine; the leverage wrapper is the problem
points.body: NISA's math: unleveraged private credit loans deliver roughly 3% liquidity premium before fees, a genuine and healthy risk spread. Most investors access private credit through BDCs or interval funds, which layer on leverage (borrowing costs roughly SOFR plus 200 bps), compounded by the manager's high fees. That leverage cost can eat the entire premium or turn it negative. Twenty years of backtesting shows a high-yield index plus high-yield CDS (a more liquid leveraging method) consistently outperforms publicly traded BDCs.

points.h: Mass pension buyouts to insurers could embed systemic risk
points.body: Companies outsourcing entire pension liabilities to insurers (pension buyouts) looks efficient, but the U.S. PBGC is well-funded but only covers pensions staying within the corporate system. Once transferred to insurers, pensions fall under state-run, underfunded guarantee associations. Historically, consortiums of large insurers have bailed out failing small ones, but if a large insurer fails—especially as many are aggressively deploying private credit—government rescue and taxpayer losses become possible.
